items.caption:
Nvidia's CEO just quit. Here's the scam lesson for you.
Scam of the Day #5. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO this week and told staff he was unfaithful. Reports say one woman involved was a suspected Chinese intelligence asset; China denies it, and it hasn't been proven. Spies call it a "honey trap". For everyone else, it's a romance scam: the FTC says almost 70,000 people reported one in 2022, losing $1.3 billion.

3 red flags:
1. Too much love, too fast
2. They can never meet in person
3. They ask for money, gift cards or crypto

Golden rule: never send money to someone you've never met. Not sure? Search their photo, tell a friend, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

items.caption:
Family safe word against AI voice scams
AI can copy a voice from a short clip. Scammers use it to fake a call from someone you love: they sound scared, they're "in trouble", and they need money right now. The FBI's fix is simple: a secret word or phrase only your family knows.

3 easy steps:
1. Pick a random word together, in person
2. Never post it or text it
3. On a scary call, ask for the word

No word? Hang up and call back on the number you already have. A real family member always knows it.

items.caption:
Black Friday scam text: "your order is on hold" (don't tap it)
Scam of the Day #1. Fake package delivery texts were the most reported text scam in the FTC's 2024 data. The link leads to a page that asks for a small "fee" and takes your card number.

3 simple steps:
1. Don't tap the link and don't reply
2. Check your orders in the store's own app, or on a website you type in yourself
3. Forward the text to 7726 (free on most US carriers), then delete it

Golden rule: check orders in the app, never through a text link. Real orders live in the app, not in a text.

items.caption:
How to check price history and track prices before Black Friday (free)
Prices can go up before a sale, so a big "% off" isn't always a low price. Check what the item usually costs, then let the price come to you.

3 quick steps:
1. Search the exact product on Google Shopping
2. Open the price history and see the usual price
3. Turn on Track price (signed in to Google) to get an alert when it drops

Golden rule: check the history first, then buy.

Google's Track price works in the US and some other countries, not the UK. In the UK, free comparison sites such as PriceSpy show price history and send price-drop alerts. For Amazon, camelcamelcamel shows past prices and can email you at your target price. Price history shows the past, not the future. Not financial advice.

items.caption:
Gift card scam: anyone who asks you to pay with a gift card is a scammer
Scam of the Day #4. The FTC says no real business or government agency will ever tell you to buy a gift card to pay them. The story changes (your boss, a business, a government agency), but the ask is the same.

3 simple steps:
1. Hang up or stop replying
2. Call them back on a number you already know, not the one they gave you
3. Already paid? Call the gift card company right away, keep the card and the receipt, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Some companies may be able to refund you

Golden rule: never read out the numbers on the back of a gift card, and never send a photo of them. Only scammers ask for those.

items.caption:
How to tell if an online store is fake: 3 checks before you pay
You see an ad: a big brand at a super low price. But fake stores copy real photos and logos. You get a knockoff, or nothing at all.

3 checks before you pay:
1. Search the store's name and web address + "scam", "complaint" or "review" (in a search engine, not the app with the ad)
2. Check how old the site is with a free domain lookup (ICANN Lookup). Brand new but "since 1998"? Red flag
3. Check how it wants you to pay. Gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or crypto only? Walk away

Golden rule: pay with a credit card where you can, so you can dispute the charge if nothing arrives. Not every site shows its creation date, so a missing date means check harder.

items.caption:
Verification code scam: never share the code your phone gets
That text code is a key to your account. Share it, and a scammer can pretend to be you. Anyone who asks for it is running a scam.

3 rules:
1. Someone asks for the code? It's a scam, even if they say they're your bank
2. Hang up. Call the number on the back of your card, never one they give you
3. Turn on two-step verification for your email and WhatsApp

The FTC says no real bank fraud team will call and ask for your code. It can also be a "buyer" online or a friend's hacked account. Already shared one? Call your bank now and change that password.

items.caption:
"Hi Mom, this is my new number" text scam: how to spot it and check
A text arrives from a number you don't know. It says it's your child and their phone broke. They chat for a bit, then ask for money for an urgent bill. This trick started on WhatsApp and has spread to normal texts.

3 simple steps:
1. Don't send money, and don't check using the new number
2. Call their old, saved number
3. Or ask something only they would know, like the dog's name

Golden rule: never pay a new number until you've called the old one. Not every new number is a scam, but checking takes a minute and real family won't mind.
